analysis.one_liner: Speeds cheaper generic drugs to market by curbing brand-name drug patent delaying tactics.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote; it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee until the 107th Congress ended, despite 62 cosponsors from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed the rules the Food and Drug Administration uses to approve generic drugs. It would have cut short some of the patent fights brand-name drug companies use to keep generics off the market, stripped the 180-month exclusivity reward from generic companies that sit on their approval instead of selling the drug, made it easier to win approval with different kinds of scientific tests, and required the Federal Trade Commission to investigate patent complaints filed mainly to delay competition. The Congressional Budget Office figures cited in the bill say generics cost 25 to 60 percent less than brand-name drugs, with potential savings of $8 to $10 billion a year.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who buy prescription drugs, especially seniors on fixed incomes and the uninsured who pay full price, would have gotten cheaper generic versions sooner. Generic drug makers would have gained faster market access, and insurers and government programs paying drug bills would have saved money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors, uninsured patients, generic drug makers

how_it_helps.text: The bill's own findings cite CBO estimates that generics cost 25 to 60 percent less than brand-name drugs, saving $15 to $30 per prescription, and that wider generic use could save purchasers $8 to $10 billion a year.

It would have accelerated generic approval when a court finds a brand-name patent invalid or not infringed, or when a settlement ends the patent fight, instead of letting the 30-month automatic hold run its course.

It would have taken away a first-filer generic company's 180-day exclusivity if it failed to market the drug, withdrew its challenge, or was found by the FDA and FTC to have engaged in anticompetitive conduct — closing a loophole that let generic companies and brand-name firms strike deals that delayed generic competition.

It would have required the FTC to investigate citizen petitions filed to delay competition and referred illegal conduct to the Justice Department, and made the 45-day patent-litigation window shorter and clearer so generics could reach the market faster.

It would have let the FDA approve a generic using pharmacodynamic, clinical, or in-vitro test endpoints when standard absorption testing doesn't apply, broadening how many drugs can get generic versions.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers would have lost revenue from delayed generic competition and the pay-for-delay settlement deals the bill targeted. Generic companies that sat on their 180-day exclusivity instead of launching would have forfeited it.

drawbacks.text: Brand-name companies and patent holders argued (and the bill itself acknowledges) that faster generic entry and shorter litigation windows weaken the patent incentives that fund research into new medicines; the bill tries to address this by promising a report on whether products still come to market 'consistent with the rights of patent owners.'

The bill keeps the generic industry's 180-day exclusivity system in place rather than replacing it, and its enforcement of competition relies on FDA and FTC case-by-case judgments, which can be slow and litigated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit was large and quantified — generics at 25 to 60 percent off, with $8 to $10 billion a year in potential savings — while the cost fell mainly on brand-name firms' patent-protected profits. The main honest tradeoff is that some future drug R&D revenue would have been competed away, and the bill's fixes were layered onto an already complex patent-and-approval system. On balance it was strongly pro-consumer.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and passed to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on May 16, 2001, with ten original cosponsors from both parties, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On June 1, 2001 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, which is where it stayed; the full committee never acted on it.
The bill drew 62 cosponsors, including 7 of the 223 House Republicans and the chamber's sole Independent, yet no version ever reached a committee vote or the House floor.
A year later, on May 7, 2002, the sponsor gave introductory remarks on the measure — the last recorded action before the bill died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies were better off: the patent-litigation delays, 30-month holds, and settlement deals the bill targeted all stayed in place, and generic competition kept arriving on the slower pre-existing timetable.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan at introduction — 54 of 208 House Democrats, 7 of 223 House Republicans, and the one Independent signed on — but the Republican-run committee never moved it.

industries.note: The bill targeted the tools brand-name firms use to stretch patent protection — 30-month approval holds, citizen petitions filed to delay generics, and settlements that pay generic rivals to stay off the market — so cheaper competition would have arrived sooner, cutting their patent-protected revenue.

Faster approval paths, broader bioequivalence testing options, and clearer rules after patent challenges would have let generics reach the market sooner — though firms that stockpiled their 180-day exclusivity without selling would have forfeited it, which is why the bill also polices generic-side anticompetitive conduct.
